scenes.label: STRASBOURG, JULY 1518
lines: July 1518. In Strasbourg, a woman named Frau Troffea starts dancing in the street.
There is no music, and no reason. She keeps going for days.

scenes.label: WITHIN A WEEK
lines: Within a week, more than thirty people have joined her.
By some accounts, as many as four hundred are dancing within a month.

scenes.label: THE CURE
lines: Doctors blamed hot blood. Their cure? More dancing.
The city opened guildhalls, built stages and hired musicians to keep the dancers moving.
It made things worse. Some accounts claim dancers died of exhaustion.

scenes.label: SHRINE OF ST VITUS
lines: Finally, the dancers were taken to a mountaintop shrine of Saint Vitus.
Priests gave them red shoes, and the outbreak faded.

scenes.label: WHY?
lines: Poisoned bread? Historians doubt it. Ergot poisoning causes convulsions, not days of dancing.
The leading theory is mass psychogenic illness, driven by famine, disease and fear of a saint's curse.

youtube.description:
In July 1518, Frau Troffea began dancing in the streets of Strasbourg. Within a week more than 30 people had joined her, and by some accounts as many as 400 within a month. Physicians blamed 'hot blood'; the city set aside guildhalls, built stages and hired musicians, which made it worse. Dancers were later taken to a shrine of St Vitus near Saverne. Reports of deaths come from later accounts and are disputed. Historian John Waller argues it was mass psychogenic illness amid famine and disease; ergot poisoning is widely doubted. The opening picture shows the dancing pilgrimage at Molenbeek after Pieter Bruegel the Elder (1564), not Strasbourg itself. Opening photo from Wikimedia Commons (credit below); all other visuals are original illustrations.
